the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all a warm thanks to the secretariat, which has been very active and helpful with all the colleagues in the committee in drawing up this draft. we are now handing the commission a series of reflections, the result of careful and concerted deliberation by the entire committee on international trade. our committee wants a more effective and democratic world trade organization, ready, from the point of view of its institutional functioning, to perform the important task of regulating international trade, and for this to happen, reform is indispensable. the recent entry of many new members - china and the imminent accession of russia - highlights the success of the organisation, which now has 152 member countries. but that is precisely why, with its new dimension, a reflection on its reorganization is necessary. in the report we emphasize the vital aspects of understanding what the wto and trade multilateralism mean in terms of a new, stronger, more dynamic and more democratic character. our agenda is filled with the doha round negotiations, an agreement which we know is always around the corner but which has not yet been reached. the committee on international trade, therefore, aware of this problem, reiterates its support for the negotiations which must lead to a success for a more balanced and fair trade, but at the same time believes that the time has come to look forward to the post-doha with courage and ambition. in passing on our views to the commission, we ask the community executive to have the same courage and the same ambition to take a political initiative in geneva which could open the way to a review of the functioning of certain mechanisms which are objectively not working today. an institutional structure is needed which can improve on the present situation by distinguishing between activities linked to the negotiation of new international rules and new commitments linked to the implementation of existing agreements. the principle of consensus is and must remain the rule in ministerial conferences, but we must also think of ways other than unanimity in the procedures leading to the final decision of an organization which, having grown larger, needs a different step. we have thought this for europe, we must think this for the wto! the guiding principle of the doha round was to involve all the member states in negotiations on a plurality of issues, in a large organization such as ours, this formula must be revised with a plurilateral approach, a kind of variable geometry. we spoke of this in the past for europe, and it is necessary today for the wto! development is an important issue, and in recent years the group of developing countries has become increasingly large and diverse, and includes emerging countries and others already largely emerged, think of china, india, brazil, south africa. it is therefore in the interests of the countries which are still developing that clearer and more homogeneous groupings should be established which correspond to the evolution of the economic situation and require everyone to take on the responsibility and commitment appropriate to their economic strength. the wto secretariat, although prestigious and competent, and we have consulted it many times during these months of work, is institutionally limited: the role of the european parliament should be strengthened, with the possibility of taking initiatives and suggesting compromises. strengthening the secretariat means giving it a geographical representativeness which makes it feel like the centre and the driving force of action and organisation, in the interests of all its members, including those developing countries which today are not sufficiently taken into account for genuine development. transparency and the parliamentary dimension: we need to increase transparency in international dispute resolution procedures to strengthen our image abroad. the promotion of a parliamentary dimension to the wto must take advantage of the existing parliamentary conference on the wto to create a genuine parliamentary assembly with consultative powers that legitimize its work. competition and coordination with other international organizations is absolutely necessary, and we must therefore also strengthen relations with international labour organizations and with certain un agencies, because social and environmental issues of great international importance cannot remain outside the scope of the wto's activities. we must not forget that we must make trade disputes the norm and the strongest aspect without taking into account that if we do not find a way to streamline and speed up these procedures, we risk having annual disputes with a detriment to companies, to member countries and to consumers. we therefore warmly urge the commission to have the same courage as the committee of this parliament in identifying new rules to make the future of the world health organization more flexible.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the policies for the promotion of human rights are first and foremost the result of the effective powers of international policy which this european union has. unfortunately, too often, as in the report which we unanimously adopted in committee, european policy is in fact national policy, and it is difficult to have a european human rights policy when national interests are so important. but it is also true that when there is the political will, and sometimes it is achieved thanks to this european parliament, which has no powers in international politics, important steps can be taken. let 's see about the death penalty: the three resolutions of this european parliament have finally dragged and won over a european position which is important for the moratorium on executions which was won in december at the united nations in new york. we see how this parliament proposed a european policy on the tibet question in the resolution we adopted at the last part-session. there are also human rights instruments, but too often the european union does not respect its own legality. we have clauses on respect for human rights in all our cooperation agreements, but we do not have effective monitoring and suspension mechanisms, because those clauses really do allow us to assert respect for democracy in third countries. we have often, as europe, criticised the united states of america in recent years because the way of promoting democracy through the military instrument has proved ineffective. and that's the truth! but it is also true that we must have alternative instruments. it is not enough to say that weapons do not work, because otherwise we give in to the pacifist, neutralist temptation, but we simply say that they may be objectively useful to dictators. the weapon we have identified, and which this report explicitly mentions - and i am very sorry that there is actually an amendment from the socialist group which wants to delete this part - is the weapon of non-violence, gandhian non-violence as a political instrument, not as a folkloric appeal, non-violence based on right, making the right live, for the life of the right, for the right to life, based on knowledge. nonviolence is also a technology and so we propose in this report that 2010 be designated the european year of nonviolence, that the european union, together with the commission and the council, promote the instruments of nonviolence by helping dissidents, an active policy, by helping democratic opposition. this is essential if we are to go beyond a mere formal defence of the human rights texts in the document, and to make human rights a reality in dictatorships and non-democracies.
member of the commission. − mr president, it is of course a great pleasure that i can again participate today in the joint discussion in plenary about two key reports in the field of human rights and democracy: the cappato report on the eu annual report on human rights and the salafranca/de keyser report on election observation missions (eoms). i would like to congratulate the three rapporteurs on their excellent work. i also welcome the fact that the two reports on human rights and on election observation are discussed jointly because i think this is a living proof of our shared conviction that human rights and democracy go hand in hand and should not be considered separate. human rights are the foundation of democracy, and democracy is indispensable to protect and promote human rights. let me address the two issues on our agenda today one after the other. obviously i am only giving a general overview here but i am ready, of course, to go into more detail afterwards in the debate. election observation is a success story of european union foreign policy and thank you, mrs de keyser, for what you have said. as a result, i think, of consistent, rigorous methodology and independent, impartial long-term observation, the eu ranks among the most credible international observer organisations. this was confirmed in recent eu observation missions to delicate election processes such as, for instance, kenya (that was mr lambsdorff), pakistan (mr gahler) and nepal (mr mulder). upcoming missions include cambodia and rwanda, both recovering from a very painful past. as in 2007, these missions will be financed in full respect of the agreed budgetary framework. the well-established cooperation between the eu eoms and the european parliament combines technical expertise with political sensitivity and ensures that the eu speaks with one voice. i would therefore again like to congratulate all chief observers so far for their outstanding work. in fact, the professionalism of the european union eoms has been a top priority for me since the beginning of my term of office, during which there have been chief observers in some 36 countries. i agree that eu election observation cannot be a stand-alone policy but must be part of a broader human-rights and democracy-support strategy. there is a need for enhancing political and technical follow-up to eu eoms. we all have to play a role and the commission will use the forthcoming review of the country strategy papers to devise more coherent policy approaches at country level, as suggested in the report, to ensure that our actions in the fields of protection and promotion of human rights, democracy promotion, electoral support and development assistance aiming at improving democratic governance and the rule of law are mutually reinforcing. there is certainly room for further improvement of the policy. i will continue to do so in close dialogue with parliament. in this context i propose to hold a second joint seminar on election observation in the autumn, building on our successful meeting last year which pointed to the essential issue of follow-up as well as of sustaining the quality of the observation work. in these areas we have already taken important steps: eu eoms are now systematically thought into the electoral cycle and there is an increasing awareness for integrating recommendations of eu eoms into dialogue with partner countries. the two entirely reviewed methodological guidelines which have just been released, as well as the continuous support to training programmes for observers, will help us to sustain the thorough high-quality work by the chief observers and their teams on the ground. the second seminar could focus on enhanced visibility for eu eoms and the political dimension of the election support. we can, of course, discuss possible further opening of our missions, as mentioned by mrs de keyser. so far we already include observers for instance from switzerland, canada and norway. i will try to be short on the second part because our council president has already said a lot. this year is an important year for human rights as we celebrate the 60th anniversary of the universal declaration of human rights and the 15th anniversary of the world conference on human rights. i think what we should say is that the past year has been characterised by the pivotal changes seen within the un human rights systems with the finalisation of the institutional design of the human rights council. now the first round of universal periodic reviews (uprs) has come to a close and the second round started on 5 may. with both some eu member states and third countries under scrutiny, i think it will be very useful to analyse in a detailed manner whether this key innovation will contribute positively to enhancing the human rights council’s effectiveness. the relevant eu council group (cohom) – this is in geneva – has started to improve coordination in view of a more coherent eu position in the human rights council and will discuss in detail conclusions to be drawn from the first two rounds. i am not going to go into all the details the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union often deals with human rights violations outside its territory and does not realise that our policies contribute to the systematic violation of rights outside the european union. for these reasons, we think that the fundamental rights agency should extend its mandate to countries which have concluded stabilization or association agreements or even countries which have concluded readmission agreements with the european union. we think this is important for migrants and asylum seekers, who are often expelled from our countries and sent to places where individual freedoms and fundamental rights are not guaranteed. we can also speak of the country which is currently holding the presidency, slovenia, where citizens are considered to have been deleted from the registers and therefore deprived of their citizenship and are sent to countries such as kosovo or serbia where their safety is not guaranteed. we are also concerned that international cooperation in the fight against terrorism has lowered the level of protection of fundamental freedoms and it is for these reasons that the opinion of the libe committee on this report is an opinion which strongly calls for the implementation of all the provisions envisaged by this parliament, in particular on cia flights and the illegal detention of alleged terrorists.
i am not saying that the european parliament should be the only institution in the world to have a right to vote, but i am saying that it should be the only institution in the world to have the right to vote. the european union has long seemed to be deliberately immune to regimes that violate human rights, interested only in deepening trade and economic relations. the commission is increasingly being drained of the council and the member states in its strategies for promoting human rights in the world. we have been witnessing a conscious renationalisation of powers in the field of the promotion of fundamental rights for some time. the commission has never been so weak in its proposals on human rights and democracy in the world as it is today, as demonstrated, for example, by the rejection of the general use of the democratic clause voted by parliament two years ago. human rights have once again become a dependent variable of economic or military control policies, as evidenced by the so-called fight against terrorism of the bush administration. it is therefore important that the european parliament continue to play a stimulating role in this area, as mrs cappato's report does. of course, the report focuses exclusively on what i would call the individualistic dimension of rights. the same rapporteur voted against our amendments which sought to show that the promotion of the development of peoples and their social, economic and cultural rights, as defined by the un, is a condition for the enjoyment of individual rights. it is the very concepts of interdependence, of indivisibility of rights, that define this concept. the rapporteur has once again abandoned himself to the black lists of countries, in which the usual countries are attacked and the most powerful member of the commission. − mr president, because i did not speak on human rights issues earlier, i will now try to come up with a few ideas. i would like to add something on human rights. human the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am replying to some of my colleagues who are not here, but i would like to make a point. the report talks about minority rights, it talks about religious freedom and of course it does not talk about respect for human rights within the european union simply because that is not the mandate of this report. i think we have done so in some way, because we have not simply made a list of criticisms of the world, we have spoken about ourselves, about how we use - for good or ill - the instruments we have, about respect for the legality of the european union, when we say that the human rights clauses are not sufficiently applied and we talk about ourselves! on behalf of the green group in the european parliament. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the green group's word on the ex-stubb report is transparency. there is no doubt that there is a tendency - and we have heard some of its representatives here - to underestimate, probably in good faith, the effects and effectiveness of the work of the lobbies, even in ways that none of us serious, in good faith, sympathetic and respectful of others can even imagine. the facts are clear and they come out again every day: for example, we have known for a few weeks that there are 34 officials within the commission who are paid directly by private companies. a recent study showed that most groups - not just mine but probably others - have excluded themselves from the vote. it also showed that the majority of the amendments tabled on reach are lobbyist in origin. it is also clear that among the officials who assist the work of members of parliament, there are some who work or have worked for companies in certain committees who now come to work for us as national experts and of course the members do not know this. so let us say that the lobbying issue is not over with the work we are doing today and i believe that commissioner kallas's work is not over with the report we are adopting today. that is why we have absolutely and convincingly supported all those amendments and all the work that has been done by everyone, including the socialist group, the group of the european people's party and the liberal group, on those amendments and those texts which seek to improve this situation and to make transparency easier. but there are still problems with this stubb report which we hope to be able to resolve by voting. the first is the lawyers' theme: when lawyers work with us and try to influence legislation, they're lobbyists, even when they're giving legal advice. we hope that this amendment will be rejected. then there is the issue of defining when this code of conduct should come into force, and it must come into force before the next european elections, otherwise we will be dealing with another issue for an excessively long period of time. finally, mr president, i think that the lobbying issue cannot be resolved by saying that we do not like it, that we criminalise lobbying, but we think that the problem of transparency is knowing who the people are, what they do and who pays them. so the problem of financial disclosure is a subject which is probably not very clear in this report but which may become so, and on this i agree with mr carnero with the work that the working party that will be set up will have to do.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i agree that we need a compulsory register, a register with a code of conduct for lobbyists, but one that applies to all the institutions and, above all, i dare say, to the commission. it is obviously essential that the code of ethics should provide for penalties in the event of misconduct and the obligation of financial transparency. it is important that these tools should be easily accessible and thus searchable via the internet. the friedrich report acknowledges that thousands of lobbyists seek to influence the decisions of the institutions, although it must be acknowledged that on a number of occasions they inform and detail members of parliament about different aspects of the measures. i am not, as those who know me know, inclined to be influenced by anyone, but that does not mean that in order to ensure independent decisions, to monitor activities which often also have the intention of influencing the allocation of community funds and the monitoring and application of legislation, it is necessary to operate in full compliance with strict ethical criteria. i shall therefore vote in favour of the fredrich report.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the inclusion of the new article 149 in the treaty of lisbon is a recognition of the important economic and social role played by sport. the detailed report by mr manolis mavrommatis highlights the many areas of interest to sport, and i should like to focus on a few in particular. first, the relationship between sport and health: although it is now widely recognised that physical activity is essential for maintaining good health, there is a worrying trend in some member states of the european union to reduce the number of hours devoted to sport in schools. this, combined with poor nutrition, creates an army of obese children, with possible negative repercussions on their physical condition. sport as an original and fun way to learn a language: i was aware of the efficient organization and spread in britain of study holidays for the learning of shakespeare's language through the practice of various sports disciplines as far back as the early 1970s. sport should support the brotherhood of peoples, unfortunately it is not always so: we regularly witness scenes of unspeakable violence in and out of stadiums, especially in football. amateur and professional sport, uncontaminated and unpolluted sport, sport as a means of personal development, as a means of cohesion and solidarity between peoples: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the hope remains that the white paper on sport will be a timely denunciation designed to bring about a decisive reversal of the trend and to recover too much insensitivity and too many culpable omissions.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to thank the rapporteur for the excellent work he has done on a report which aims to give strategic guidance on the role of sport in the european union. sport is a social phenomenon which has always generated values such as solidarity, team spirit and identity, as stated in the declaration on the total importance of sport annexed to the treaty of amsterdam. sport helps to develop physical, intellectual and social skills, so sport should be practised both in the education system and in other aspects of social life. the practice of sport for the disabled is not to be underestimated: all member states, local and regional authorities and sports organisations should ensure and facilitate access to sports facilities for disabled people. in contemporary society, sport faces new threats such as the exploitation of young players, doping, racism, violence and money laundering. the problem of violence is not only inside the stadium, but also outside. i welcome the commission's commitment to preventing unrest by facilitating dialogue with member states, international organisations, sports organisations and law enforcement. it is also important to stress the economic side of sport. discriminatory tax regimes applied in the member states in favour of players may have distortive effects on competition. rules are therefore needed to ensure a competitive balance between sports clubs.

in writing. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome the frassoni reports on the new comitology procedures. the new powers granted to parliament in the 'merit' procedure with a right of scrutiny, which allow members to block the progress of a text approved by the committee if the experts have not respected their mandate, is a major success for parliament and an important step towards rebalancing the powers of the european institutions. i agree that the efficiency of the procedure should be improved by making the committee's decisions more accessible and clearer. i am also in favour of the establishment of an electronic register which will allow greater control over decisions taken in comitology. i certainly think it is essential that the limitations on the three-month period for the ep's right of scrutiny be limited to exceptional cases only, in line with the letter of the interinstitutional agreement of july 2007: the shortening of the time limit should be granted only in cases of urgency and efficiency. some ep committees have already successfully tested the effectiveness of the threat of vetoes to get immediate answers and clarifications from the commission. i therefore believe that this is an instrument which parliament will have to use more and more to exercise political control over the decisions of the technicians.
in writing. - i am voting in favour of the report on the protection of human rights, since we are still too often witnessing violations of these rights. the european union includes them among its fundamental principles to the extent that respect for human rights is rightly a prerequisite for accession to the european union. the european union therefore has a responsibility to act as a guarantor of these rights in europe and in non-european countries, through a coherent common foreign policy, independent of the interests and positions of the member states, by promoting the ratification of the statute of the international criminal court throughout the world to protect individuals from so-called crimes against humanity and to prevent genocide and other atrocities from being committed in the future without fear of impunity, and by increasing the effectiveness and efficiency of the unhcr. i also think it is important that the un resolution on a universal moratorium on the death penalty be followed up. the european union must also contribute to the respect of human rights vis-à-vis important trading partners. i hope that china will eliminate the practice of torture as an important sign of openness to a culture of respect for human rights, consistent with the spirit of peace which has always been the symbol of the olympic games.
in writing. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i support this report because i am convinced that free trade is a necessary step towards global well-being. however, our support for any supranational economic agreement can only be based on strict rules which in effect bind the parties to ratify the fundamental ilo conventions, thus guaranteeing the protection and defence of workers. the rapporteur recalled that asean as a whole is the eu's fifth largest trading partner, which highlights the many commercial interests in this region, which is certainly a fast-growing market. this strong presence and the absence of effective local legislation in the field of employment oblige us, through the new agreement, to provide for strict regulation not only of an economic nature but, above all, of a social, environmental and human rights nature, thus also limiting the effect of 'dumping'. the safety of products, the protection of workers and the environment cannot and must not be jeopardized by any kind of purely economic agreement. we all have a moral and institutional obligation to find the courage to be much more rigorous and selective in the choice of our trading partners, so that europe can be an example for the rest of the world.

in writing. - the report by mr manolis mavrommatis on the white paper on sport. in fact, i recognise the important role that sport plays in the life of each person and in society, as it is a means through which the individual overcomes personal challenges, discovers his passions and talents, identifies himself in a group, understands the importance of respecting the rules: extending these values internationally, it is understood how sport can break down geographical barriers and promote social relations and peace. i think it is appropriate to stress that any kind of transgression in sport of the rules of civil and moral ethics, such as doping, deliberate racist acts or gambling, must be punished by seeking, as a preventive measure, to recover the ideal of sport and its ultimate goal. finally, i would like to remind you that the growing importance of certain sports at the expense of others is often justified by the large disparity in the salaries of players in different sports. in this connection, i believe that some support measures should be introduced for the less widespread and less well-known sports.

the agenda includes the report by sergio berlato, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation amending regulation (ec) no 1782/2003 as regards the transfer of tobacco aid to the community tobacco fund for the years 2008 and 2009 and regulation (ec) no 1234/2007 as regards the financing of the community tobacco fund (com (2008) 0051 - c6-0062/2008 - 2008/0020 (cns)) (a6-0164/2008).
the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the european commission's proposal essentially provides for the 5% deduction on tobacco-related aid to be extended for the 2008-2009 marketing year and for these funds to be used to continue financing the community tobacco fund, which exclusively funds information programmes aimed at improving european citizens' knowledge of the harmful effects of the consumption of tobacco products. i think it is appropriate to emphasize a few objective elements of the evidence. the transfer of resources from cap aid to the fund is a rare and positive example of integration and cooperation between the agricultural and health policies of the european union. as the fund's work is important for the citizens of the union, and will remain important in the years to come, as the commission has also stressed, we do not believe that it can be expected to cease its financial support in 2007 or 2009. the deduction made from coupled aid granted to farmers has always been the sole source of financing for the community tobacco fund. the financial basis of this deduction has been considerably reduced by the reform of the tobacco cmo and by the choice made by some member states to apply total decoupling, totally uncoupling these resources from the deduction to the fund. it is necessary to provide, through a further extension of the period of application of the deduction and an increase in the percentage of the deduction, that sufficient financial resources are made available to the programmes and the fund without any additional expenditure to the union budget at least until the end of the current financial perspective, while also seeking other sources of funding for the fund. other positive aspects of the fund's mechanism of action include the provision for co-financing by proven proposers of at least 25% of the total amount of approved projects, thus increasing the availability of resources. the committee on agriculture has dealt with these issues on a number of occasions and remains committed to strengthening the measures against smoking and to improving the communication to the public on the harmful effects of smoking on human health. on the other hand, we are fully aware, as already documented in the legislative resolution of the european parliament of 10 march 2004, that the level of european production of raw tobacco, now further reduced and concentrated in a few specific areas of the union, represents less than 4% of world production and has no impact on local consumption of tobacco products. although this is not the subject of today's debate, it should be remembered that the european union is the world's leading importer of raw tobacco and that it sources more than 70% of its needs from third countries, with tobacco often produced under less controlled conditions than the european product, mainly from brazil, malawi, argentina, indonesia, zimbabwe, india and china, also resulting in a trade deficit of more than eur 1.2 billion a year. on the other hand, in the member states where tobacco aid has already been completely decoupled, in addition to the cancellation of transfers to the fund, there has been a total abandonment of tobacco production without any economically and employment-friendly alternatives emerging, with very serious negative impacts on the entire rural area concerned and without causing, as was logically expected, any change in local consumption of tobacco products. as regards the proposal to apply a deduction to aid for the 2008 calendar year, taking into account that the cultivation contracts for the 2008 tobacco harvest have already been concluded, the committee on agriculture considers that acceptance of this proposal could generate a large number of legal actions and litigation which would ultimately result in serious damage only to agricultural producers. the committee on agriculture considers that the extension of the withholding until the 2012 marketing year and the increase in the rate of withholding in favour of the fund to 6% make it possible to provide sufficient financial resources for the european tobacco fund until the year 2013 and calls on the commission to draw up a multiannual programme which, thanks to the amendments introduced by the amendments tabled here, will be able to count on an amount of over eur 81 million without any burden for the union budget.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would first of all like to congratulate the rapporteur on his excellent work. this report has two objectives: strengthen tobacco control actions by extending the funding of the european tobacco fund and at the same time align the tobacco sector with the other cmos that will expire naturally with the 2012 campaign. we must not forget, however, that the fight against smoking must not be conducted by eliminating tobacco cultivation in europe, since the european union is the world's leading importer of raw tobacco and sources more than 75% of its needs from third countries, to the benefit of tobacco often produced without health control guarantees. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat tobacco smoking in the community.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there are certain facts which are not in dispute. the first: it is certain that total decoupling reduces production. the second: the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat tobacco production in the community. the third element is the fact that we are putting hundreds and thousands of people on the hunger list without any concrete results. i therefore believe that tobacco aid should be used to explain to consumers the harmful effects of smoking - and from this point of view it is peaceful that the money comes from aid - and at the same time we must enable tobacco growers to quit, but slowly and with the necessary time from the entire sector. i therefore ask that the berlato report be voted on.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to thank the speakers and the commissioner. i would remind you that, as regards the future of the european tobacco sector, the recent formal request to the commission, signed by the ministers of almost all the producing member states, including the countries which have opted for total decoupling and the new member states, is that the commission itself should present a proposal for a regulation to extend the current estimates of support for tobacco until the year 2013. i believe that this issue will necessarily have to be addressed in the context of the current debate on the health check of the cap. i conclude, mr president, by inviting my colleagues - who at first sight might seem less interested in a measure which concerns only a deduction on aid to farmers in the five old member states - who have kept aid partially coupled, to reflect on the fact that the use of these resources and the information work of the fund will continue to be used for the benefit of the health of all the citizens of the union. i also want to point out that we may be experiencing a fundamental misunderstanding: the report does not deal with the extension of aid to tobacco producers, and it does not decide on this, but simply votes on a report which talks about an extension of the financing of the community tobacco fund. as regards the extension of aid, it will be a decision to be taken in the future, but the subject of the report is quite different and concerns the extension of the community tobacco fund funding and not the extension of tobacco farmers' funding in the immediate and near future.

directive 2004/38 is based on well-established principles of union law. many of these arrangements have been in place for decades. the directive also incorporates the case law of the court of justice on these issues. following romania's accession to the european union, romanians enjoy the same freedom of movement as other union citizens. romanians are no longer immigrants from third countries. romanians are citizens of the union. they may in no case be treated less favourably than other citizens of the union. and the commission will make sure that their rights are respected. the directive allows member states to refuse the right of residence in the territory of inactive union citizens who do not have sufficient resources in order not to become a burden on their social assistance system. the assessment of this resource condition cannot be automatic, but must take account of the individual's personal behaviour. the rules on free movement are not made to benefit criminals. the directive allows the exclusion of persons whose behaviour represents a real, present and sufficiently serious threat to the fundamental interests of society. the fight against crime must be conducted in full respect of the rule of law. a decision to exclude may only be taken on a case-by-case basis and the procedural guarantees and substantive conditions must be respected. in the case of immediate exclusion, the urgency shall be duly justified. the exclusion of citizens of the union is an extreme measure. this is a limitation of a fundamental freedom of the treaty. the essential aspects of roma in writing. − the latest intergovernmental conference on climate change and the various conferences under the united nations framework convention on climate change (unfccc) have shown that man-made greenhouse gases are the cause of climate change and that the rise in global temperature to + 2°c above pre-industrial levels must be stopped. i therefore agree with the committee on climate change and the rapporteur in calling for more stringent action and more studies on the effects of climate change, monitoring phenomena such as desertification, glacier melting, changes in the marine environment, catastrophic atmospheric events, etc. the latest reports from the european environment agency indicate that much more needs to be done to meet the kyoto targets and the additional reduction targets set by the eu council in march 2007. in the light of the energy and climate package, the communication on limiting climate change to 2°c, i believe, however, that further measures can be taken to improve 'energy efficiency' which would allow for significant savings in greenhouse gas emissions. this is also done through a labelling system which indicates the environmental footprint in relation to the greenhouse gas parameter. i believe that individuals, european citizens and people in third countries, should be more directly involved in promoting awareness and active participation in the fight against climate change through small energy saving actions.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the damage caused by the use of depleted uranium is so great that it would be very inappropriate to call it collateral damage. the damage is spread in successive waves to the enemy soldiers affected and to the same soldiers who use it: the gulf syndrome, the balkan syndrome. then, for decades to come, it is the civilian populations living in theatres of war who inhale it, ingest it, contaminate water tables and the food chain, and suffer the radiation. the most serious damage from exposure to heavy metal radiation is borne by children, growing bodies and especially those in the womb. the exponential increase in genetic malformations and childhood cancers in areas affected by uranium use is evidence of this. a recent bbc study showed that within 24 hours of the massive bombing of the balkans, atmospheric radioactivity detection points in northern england were at an all-time high. it is therefore proposed not only to ban depleted uranium but also to prosecute for war crimes those who use it, knowing and knowing the consequences, and those who will do so when a ban is imposed.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has already made a number of proposals. the commission has figures which show that more than 8 000 people are killed and 300 000 injured on the roads of the european union every year. this is an intolerable situation and that is why we have been working hard for some years to make road traffic safer. the european parliament adopted a proposal for a pedestrian protection directive a few years ago, which was then adopted in 2003. this was one of the first pieces of legislation in the world to be specifically designed to protect pedestrians. this legislation has obliged manufacturers to design new vehicles more pedestrian-friendly and to demonstrate this in appropriate tests. since then, legislation has been adopted, not least under pressure from the european parliament, to counter the danger posed by frontal protection bars to unprotected road users. the existing legislation on pedestrian protection recognises that it may be difficult to meet the requirements laid down therein. the commission has undertaken to examine the feasibility of these requirements and the possibilities of using new active safety systems. the commission has commissioned a study to this end, the results of which you are aware, and this study confirms the assumption that in some respects the requirements could not be met and that active safety systems are also suitable for improving pedestrian protection. the commission has therefore put forward the proposal which you are debating today, and that is a proposal for a combination of passive safety systems with a brake assistant, the installation of which should be made compulsory. this will provide an even higher level of protection. the commission estimates that the proposal will result in about 1100 fewer deaths on our roads each year. the commission will of course continue to work on the implementation of similar rules at international level once the proposal has been adopted. let me mention a few key elements of the proposal: the commission's proposed regulation sets achievable requirements for passive safety and makes it compulsory for vehicles to be equipped with an active safety system, known as brake assist. the commission has also proposed that the rules on pedestrian protection should now also apply to off-road cars, so-called suvs. this combination will significantly improve the safety of unprotected road users. the regulation summarises the tests required for vehicles and frontal protection buckles to demonstrate adequate protection of pedestrians. the requirements to be met by the tests shall be laid down in implementing measures to this regulation. the commission also proposes to extend the scope of the regulation to include active systems, which it considers can bring significant safety benefits now and in the future, and to remove the weight limit for passenger cars and light commercial vehicles to which the regulation is intended to apply. i should like to thank in particular your rapporteur, mr ferrari, for his efforts to ensure that the proposal is revised and adopted by consensus. this is how we have managed to reach a consensus on this proposal. the report by mr ferrari supports the commission's proposal, for which i am very grateful, and the amendments you have proposed will indeed help to clarify certain points. mr ferrari, you propose to continue to monitor and examine the use and improvement of passive safety systems and the possible use of new active safety systems and then, if necessary, to propose amendments to the existing legislation. the commission is willing to do so and will do so. other amendments are intended to ensure that the requirements of the regulation become applicable to the vehicles concerned as early as possible and to allow manufacturers sufficient time to make the necessary design changes. the fact is that for a whole series of european vehicles the new requirements mean that substantial changes have to be made to the design of the vehicles, so that major design changes are necessary. i am pleased to inform you that all the amendments proposed in mr ferrari's report are acceptable to the commission. the commission is confident that the proposal can now be adopted at first reading, given the importance of the regulation for improving road safety and the timetable for introducing the tests provided for in it.
the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, we have reached the final stage of this regulation on the protection of pedestrians and vulnerable road users. the aim of this regulation is to transform the safety requirements for pedestrians and other vulnerable road users in the event of injuries due to a collision with a motor vehicle. the scope of this regulation is significant because it absorbed two previous directives, one from 2003 and the other from 2005. the first directive set out the safety requirements for cars, which were to be implemented in two stages. the first phase started in 2005 and the requirements of the second phase have not been technically feasible for all vehicles. the second directive concerns the use of frontal protection systems on vehicles and sets out various levels of protection for vulnerable road users in the event of a collision with vehicles equipped with such systems. among the most sensitive points i would mention the bas, brake assist system: it is a system that will reduce road deaths by 35%. but the biggest victory was probably to have achieved the application of this instrument within 24 months of the entry into force of the regulation for all categories of cars, from small commercial vehicles to suvs and larger vehicles which are often, because of their large mass, those which will cause the greatest physical damage to citizens. it was not easy at first, partly because the car industry needs industrial, physiological time to implement certain measures. but i am glad that the issue and the sensitivity of the matter have been understood by all parties and i appreciate the efforts made to put this system into practice. a second aspect of the regulation was that of frontal protection systems. the 2005 directive will be absorbed by this regulation and therefore cars that decide to fit so-called 'bul-bars' will not be type-approved if the safety requirements for frontal protection systems do not guarantee the same level of safety and therefore for vehicles without frontal protection systems. i am aware, however, that we have certainly done a great deal, but much more can be done, particularly as research will increasingly be directed towards improving the safety of pedestrians and vulnerable road users. i have felt the need to leave a door open for improvements to this text. i am referring in particular to collision avoidance systems. there are currently no effective articulation systems for pedestrian safety on the market, but in a few years they could be developed. that is why it provides that if, five years after the entry into force of this regulation, as the commissioner said, the industry is able to present passive safety systems to ensure the safety of pedestrians, the commission will have to submit a new text to parliament and the council which takes account of the technical arrangements. the problem of security is very much felt in europe and i have personally been personally committed to sending a strong message to all the citizens of the european union. the very delicacy of the matter led me to ensure that the regulation was adopted at first reading, avoiding a second reading with the council which would have had the sole consequence of pushing back the date of entry into force of the regulation too much. this position was also shared by my colleagues on the committee on transport. all the amendments tabled were aimed at protecting pedestrians and vulnerable road users in the first place. i hope, therefore, that this regulation will be the first strong signal from the european parliament to the european parliament to adopt ever more stringent rules on road safety in europe, showing that europe is united, alive and close to its citizens.

insist on carrying out their own ratification procedures? why is it that we insist on coming back to the reasons why we started this whole debate on a new treaty for the european union? i hope you will allow me to say a few words about this because, do not forget, the european leaders have invested a lot of political capital in this whole procedure. it has taken a long time and a lot of energy to discuss the underlying issues and the problems behind the need for a new treaty to design a new machinery for a european union that has changed so dramatically in a short period of time. let me just mention three reasons why we think a new treaty is needed. firstly, it would give the charter of fundamental rights legally binding force. europe is not only about the internal market – as somebody said here – but also about the rights of persons and the rights of workers. a second reason is, of course, that we would like to be able to speak with one single strong voice in the world, to be stronger on the international scene, and to do that on the basis of our values. we would like to stand up on the international scene, to fight for sustainable development, to discuss oil prices, conflict prevention and other important issues. this is one of the reasons behind the discussion on a new treaty. the third reason is, of course, to make the european union more democratic. how ironic it is, for those who talk about respecting the ‘no’ and about the outcome, that the treaty would actually give more power to the directly elected european parliament. it would mean more involvement of the national parliaments and would mean that the council has to hold its deliberations in public, with the citizens’ initiative as one of the important elements in a chapter on participatory democracy, which is a new improvement in the treaty. the t-shirt party up there have the text ‘respect the “no”’. my idea of doing that includes knowing the concerns of the irish people. it is understanding why they voted ‘no’. they have made their own interpretations but i think it is very important that the irish government, with the help of our eurobarometer opinion polls, can better understand what the concerns are and whether we can do something about them. is that not the idea of democracy? that is the way forward – to understand their arguments, to work with the other member states and also to get their respect for the problems that we can, hopefully, solve together. as we did after the ‘no’ vote in the french and dutch referendums, we have already carried out a eurobarometer survey, which i think will also help better to understand the challenges of any referendum. carrying out a referendum has its upsides but also its downsides – or rather, from a democratic point of view, challenges. after the voters have been presented with such a complex wide text as a new international treaty, of course there is room for different interpretations of the results. we need to understand better what the irish said, what they are afraid of and what they hope for. i already understand from the preliminary results that this is not a general ‘no’ to europe. it is also understanding and respecting their role in a european union. the upside of carrying out a referendum is that you also have to inform and communicate with citizens, with all the challenges that implies. i think that everybody can see that we also have to analyse what we can improve in terms of communication and information to citizens. i have always said that communication is a tool for democracy. this must be based on a right for citizens to know what goes on at european level, what is decided and how citizens can have a say. that work has to be further intensified and that is why also the commission will continue with what we started a couple of years ago, called plan ‘d’, as in debate, dialogue and democracy. that will be based on the idea of having a citizens’ ownership of eu policies...

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today, with the vote in favour of the weber report, we have taken perhaps a decisive step towards drawing up a comprehensive framework for combating illegal activities, capable of meeting the security needs of many european citizens, who are often victims of crimes committed by non-community nationals. i have noted with pleasure that the european parliament, which is the guarantor of freedom and the rights of all men, has finally expressed its support for a common policy to meet the needs of the member states in the fight against illegal immigration. it was clarified that the objective is not only to establish cases of illegality but also to ensure clear, transparent and fast return procedures. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this phenomenon, such as the ban on the use of the word 'cold' in the name of the community.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to see that i always have the admiration of many colleagues, whom i thank of course for having waited to hear why i voted in favour of this weber report. mr president, i believe that we are facing something not unlike the barbarian invasions of the roman empire 2,000 years ago and beyond. then the roman empire was invaded by armed troops and the romans defended themselves with arms but succumbed, as we all know, with great disasters. today, when people from all the other countries of the world are coming to europe - and they are right, of course, because they are hungry, the barbarians were hungry too and wanted to feed at the fountains of rome - europe has the right to defend itself and to establish that those who want to invade our territories must be returned to the frontiers.

in writing. - today, with the positive vote on the weber report, we have perhaps taken a decisive step towards drawing up a comprehensive framework for combating illegal activities which can meet the security needs of many european citizens, who are often victims of crimes committed by non-community citizens. i am pleased to note that the european parliament, the guarantor of freedom and the rights of all men, has spoken in favour of a common policy to meet the needs of the member states in the fight against illegal immigration. it was clarified that the objective is not only to establish cases of illegality but also to ensure clear, transparent and fast return procedures. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this phenomenon, such as the ban on re-entry, but also to help children. these measures require that human rights be observed in the reception centres. the fight against illegal immigration is fought above all by seeking agreements with the countries of origin, which can no longer remain passive in the face of a tragedy that is not only national but also european, and by sending a strong signal to those who are preparing to enter europe illegally. our continent is not a conquest ground for anyone and beyond rights there are duties to be respected.
in writing. - i congratulate my colleagues on the libe committee on the compromise reached with the council. this is the first time that the union has succeeded in establishing common rules for the return of third-country nationals who are staying illegally on its territory. it is commendable that the objective of the directive, in ensuring common and transparent return procedures, is to ensure humane treatment of those concerned and to improve cooperation both between national authorities of migrants and between member states, including through the establishment of a re-entry ban, valid throughout the union, not exceeding five years. voluntary return, the duration of temporary custody with the modulation provided for in different cases, the organisation of detention centres, the prohibition of collective returns, the special protection to be given to minors and vulnerable persons in adopting a return decision and the maintenance of family unity are all aspects which positively characterize the proposal for a directive, as well as free legal assistance, if required, to formalise the appeal against the expulsion decision. i voted in favour of this measure, in the knowledge that common and transparent rules will help to combat illegalities better and will help to give greater security to citizens, and i reiterated once again that on common problems, such as those linked to immigration, europe must behave in a clear way, which will ensure that reception and legality are inseparable concepts.

the chairman of the council. − the council is aware of the consequences of rising prices for european citizens, and of the negative impact of these prices on the european economy. this pressing issue has been discussed at several recent council meetings. it will also be discussed by the heads of state and government at the meeting that begins tomorrow. analysis of the causes of high oil prices suggests that they are structural. it is not expected that oil production could keep pace with the continuously increasing demand. the causes of high oil prices have been well presented by the european commission in its recent communication, so i will not go into detail. the consequences of such oil price movements are reflected in higher inflation, higher household costs and problems in many sectors in the union: agriculture, fisheries, transport and various industries. assessing that the reasons for the increase in oil prices are structural and that this trend is likely to continue, we need to look for long-term solutions within the union: promoting competitiveness in energy markets, increasing the transparency of the oil market and, above all, improving energy efficiency and diversifying the energy supply. on energy efficiency, the european council in march last year set a target of 20% energy savings by 2020. the directive on energy end-use efficiency and energy services, adopted in 2006, also contributes to this objective. but legislation alone cannot achieve everything. we can do a lot with more rational households, more rational businesses. the council and parliament may also encourage this by regularly raising awareness. the second measure mentioned concerns the diversification of energy supply. i would remind you that in this context the spring european council last year adopted an action plan for an energy policy for europe. the commission has also taken into account the fact that the aid is not limited to the minimum necessary to achieve the objective of the aid. i mention all this because i want to emphasise that the union has already taken some necessary measures over the past years to reduce the sensitivity of the european economy to rising oil prices in the longer term. of course, these existing policies will need to be upgraded in the future. at its last meeting, the economic and financial affairs council (ecofin) endorsed, inter alia, the 2005 manchester agreement, according to which, in response to high oil prices, tax and other policies that distort competition and prevent economic operators from making appropriate market adjustments should be avoided. measures to mitigate the effects of higher oil prices on the poorer sections of the population must be short-term and targeted so as not to cause market disturbances. the g8 finance ministers also spoke about rising oil prices last week. among other things, they stressed that this was a global problem and that solutions had to be sought globally. i would also like to mention that at the general affairs council meeting this week, this monday, we approved the 18-month programme for the next three presidencies, and among the priorities in this programme is also the effective fight against high food and oil prices. let me conclude: we need coordinated policies to tackle these challenges, both within the european union and at international level. we must take measures with a view to avoiding creating new imbalances and problems. we are of course counting on the constructive cooperation of this parliament in the further handling of these pressing issues, particularly in the examination of legislative proposals.
member of the commission. − madam president, for me each day starts with a routine check of oil prices, and in recent times the news has been more or less in one direction: oil prices are getting higher and higher. over the last three years, prices for oil in us dollars have more than tripled. for the eu, with a 37% share in energy consumption coming from oil, it is easy to understand the actual and potential impact of the high oil prices on our economies and citizens. we have a constant decrease in our own production – and it is still substantial – but we have this decrease since the late 1990s. a continuing increase in imports consequently makes our oil dependency high and the amount that we are paying for buying energy resources is increasing all the time. this has a direct effect on our citizens and businesses. increased oil prices create inflation and that impact can be noticed already. the contribution of energy to the increase in the price index in the fourth quarter of 2007 averaged 0.8% in the euro area. this means direct, tangible impacts on households and on a lot of economic sectors, not least those who cannot pass on the price of energy to the final consumer. the increase in prices of motor and heating fuels for households between april 2007 and april 2008 exceeded by far the overall growth of consumer prices. as an example, the prices of transport fuels rose on average by 12.7% as opposed to the inflation average of 3.6%. our most vulnerable citizens are again amongst those most affected. back in september 2005, i was already talking to you about rising oil prices and i presented a five-point plan. since then we have been working out a whole series of new proposals to begin to reply to the challenge of high and growing oil prices: on energy efficiency, on cars, on fuel quality, on renewable energy. as a result of these policies, we can expect a gradual decrease in oil consumption in the eu over the coming years. we now have roughly more or less stable consumption in the last three years and the beginning of the switch to cleaner, more efficient transport that uses renewable energy sources. whilst more needs to be done, and certainly we should not underestimate the problems resulting from high energy prices for our citizens, particularly the most vulnerable households as well as many businesses, this already provides a good basis on which to further develop the best possible policy response to the challenge. indeed, the fact that oil prices have continued to rise does not mean that our policies have failed. i am convinced that without our ambitious climate and energy goals the situation would be even more difficult. but it is clear from the latest trends that we need to further step up our efforts. so let me now consider the long-term factors affecting the oil market. put simply, we are leaving the era of cheap oil, and cheap energy in general. global energy demand is growing and the international energy agency estimates that it could increase by more than 50% by 2030. in particular, emerging economies are consuming more and more energy. on the other hand, it is far from clear whether there will be sufficient oil production to satisfy global demand. experts say that geologically there are still enough resources underground for the next 40-50 years. as the international energy agency has stated, it is far from certain whether the producing countries have the ability or willingness to step up production to meet seemingly inevitable and long-term continued increases in global oil demand. the era of cheap energy is over, at a time when in any event we have an absolute obligation to future generations to move to clean, carbon-free energy sources for heat, power and transport due to climate change. this is the challenge facing us. this requires a clear response. but, before coming to the long-term and medium-term measures, i would like to mention some short-term steps alleviating the impact on consumers. the effects on the most vulnerable groups must be mitigated in the shorter term, where necessary through social measures. support to the poorest households can be justified and needed, but needs to be targeted. at the same time we should be very cautious as regards changes in the taxation regime. experience has shown that such measures, whilst in many ways politically very attractive, in fact only make the longer-term transition to dealing with high energy prices and saving carbon more difficult. it is far better to target help where it is really most needed. in terms of further developing the eu’s long-term approach to meeting the challenge, our existing energy policies are viewed by many as a ‘world leader’. the commission has always insisted that its recent climate and energy package had the combined objectives of sustainability, security of supply and competitiveness, a fact becoming clearer by the day. let me recall in more detail the most important elements of these policies, already in place or under examination in this house: the draft directive guaranteeing 20% renewables in our final energy consumption by 2020; the new rules to expand and strengthen the eu’s emissions trading system (ets), ensuring that we meet our target of a 20% greenhouse gas reduction by 2020 and establishing the ets as driver for change; the proposal for reducing co2 emissions from cars and the fuel quality directive that will oblige oil suppliers to progressively reduce their co2 and energy consumption in the products they sell; and, most importantly, the energy efficiency action plan, covering all sectors, at all levels, from the international partnership for energy efficiency cooperation to the covenant of mayors at the local level, to specific measures such as labelling of consumer goods or requirements for the energy efficiency of buildings. practically all the measures mentioned in the energy efficiency action plan are cost effective at usd 60 per barrel of oil. this represents a start, but we need to do more. the commission will therefore continue the work at international level, notably constructive dialogue between the main oil-producing and consuming countries, such as the jeddah meeting which will be convened this week in saudi arabia, or the eu-opec dialogue next week. it will scrutinise the functioning of the oil and petroleum markets in the european union and make suggestions for possible further policy action in the second strategic energy review later this year. it will assist oil-importing developing countries to mitigate short-term impacts of high fuel and food prices and to bring about structural improvements in their energy efficiency performance and the use of alternatives fuels. it will lead efforts in an increased drive for energy efficiency. this will remain my highest priority. this means better legislation internally in the eu. it also means pushing for a more effective international energy efficiency partnership, which was adopted last week at the g8 energy ministerial in japan on the initiative of the european union. the existing legislation on energy efficiency and the improvements that i will table over the coming months on buildings, labelling and minimum product standards are truly important, but have to be seen as only one of many measures needed. the real challenge is the effective implementation of energy efficiency policies at national, regional and local level throughout the european union. the commission will play a greater role in assisting member states in meeting this challenge. i shall mention biofuels, because this issue is often discussed. in the draft renewables directive we translate the commitment of the european council to ensure that 10% of eu transport is powered by renewable fuel by 2020 into practice. it should be noted that this 10% can be covered by biofuels or electricity from renewable sources, or by increasing energy efficiency in the transport fleet. i am convinced that the eu can and must generate the biofuels that it uses in a sustainable and responsible manner and not affect global food-production levels. this can be done in a sustainable way by using previous set-aside land in the eu, improving land yields in a sustainable way, investing in technology for second generation biofuels, and working together with developing countries to ensure that biofuels complement food production and not replace it. with such an approach, the development of alternative clean transport fuels must be part of the eu’s response to the challenges of oil prices and climate change. the european union will need to continue its international efforts and its dialogue with its main partners. the g8 last week and the jeddah meeting on oil prices this weekend show that the issue tops the political agenda. we should use the credibility we are building and lead international action to exploit energy efficiency potentials and clean energy production around the globe, and enable the functioning of global efficient and trustworthy commodity markets. however, action starts at home, and a renewed push for renewable energy and energy efficiency is beneficial not only for the climate but also for our economy. there is an energy future for all of us. this future will most likely be organised around different patterns of production, consumption and behaviour. as with climate change, action is needed now and the commission is fully involved in this.

the first response was always 'excessive and dangerous speed and alcohol'. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. if rising fuel prices are a problem, if energy consumption as a whole must be reduced urgently, if we want to reduce the irresponsibly high level of co2 emissions, and if we want to do something about climate change, we will not achieve this with the philosophy of always more, always higher, always faster, always more refined, always more mobile, but rather with a different lifestyle, with slower, more modest, more economical! i have one particular point to object to. the rapporteur writes: 'affordability is a key issue for consumers. many consumers simply cannot afford the systems in question. therefore, intelligent transport systems must be affordable and widely available as soon as possible. the institute for environmental and climate change research in heidelberg calculated a few years ago that an average car in germany receives about 3,000 euros a year in state or taxpayer support, when all direct and indirect transport costs are taken into account. it is not possible to support environmental damage and health risks, but on the contrary, in accordance with the principle of cost-effectiveness, those who cause damage must pay. it is not only the construction and maintenance of roads that are cost factors, but also the basic consumption and the various damages caused to nature and man. i do not want to be misunderstood, but i am not against better technology, but i am against this blind belief in technology! if we want to subsidize mobility, we should first of all support rail and local public transport, cycling and walking - that would be smarter, healthier, safer and more environmentally friendly!

member of the commission. - mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, i thank mrs mohácsi and mrs frassoni, mr wiersm, mr catani and all the other members for their questions. for the fourth time in this house, we have the opportunity to speak about the situation of roma in italy. i think that everyone in this house - across most political groups - will agree that the situation of the roma needs to be addressed by taking immediate and responsible action to overcome the social, economic and humanitarian crisis. the commission has received with considerable concern press reports that the italian authorities are taking the fingerprints of persons living in 'nomad camps' and that a database is to be created from them. in the meantime, the italian authorities have provided the commission with information on the general legal context. it follows from them that, under the state of emergency declared on 23 may, the decree of 30 may allows the mayors of rome, naples and milan to take certain measures. these measures also include 'identification and counting of persons, including minors, present in nomad camps'. it also provides that the measures implemented by the mayor must be implemented 'in accordance with the general principles of community law and directives'. the italian authorities state that these measures are taken in the interests of the people living in these camps, in particular to enable them to live in decent conditions. the commission notes the italian authorities' willingness to cooperate. this information is useful, but uncertainty remains as to the nature and real impact of the measures taken and their implementation. the taking of fingerprints and their storage in databases can only be carried out within a legal framework that strictly respects community legislation and fundamental rights. in this context, the commission requested clarification of the purpose of these activities, while respecting the principles of legality and proportionality in their implementation. the commission notes that the italian authorities have not provided any evidence that the measures in question are imputable to the state. in order to obtain a more precise picture of the legal framework in which these measures take place, the commission decided to write to the italian authorities to obtain additional information on this subject. on 7 july, the italian authorities sent the commission further information, which will be analysed. the commission is aware of the existence of social tensions in italy. at this forum, we discussed the situation of roma in italy and other countries in may. the commission stressed at the time that the real problems of poverty and social exclusion faced by roma in italy and elsewhere could not be ignored. it also underlined that this situation leads to human suffering and social tensions. to respond to this situation, it is necessary to combat crime and to find solutions that are truly relevant to the problems faced by roma, especially roma children, who are the first victims of poverty and social exclusion. roma need to be helped, not stigmatized. this is why the commission, in its report adopted last week, stressed the need for the european union, the member states and civil society to join forces to achieve effective coordination of their efforts. in conclusion, the commission, and in particular its vice-president jacques barrot, will remain in regular contact with the italian authorities, who have undertaken to provide a full report on the subject by the end of july. at the same time, the commission will continue to assess how member states have transposed directive 2004/38 of 29 april 2004 into their national law and how they are applying it in practice. i firmly believe that the italian government has the will to implement a policy of social inclusion in full respect of fundamental rights and community law.
