the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the commission, the french presidency and my colleagues in parliament, and first of all the rapporteurs for opinions, for their commitment to drafting a compromise text at first reading which will enable the safer internet programme to enter into force on schedule, i.e. as from 1 january 2009. the new programme for minors using the internet and other communication technologies, as it is known, will be structured around four main lines of action: reducing illegal or harmful content and countering harmful behaviour online; promoting a safer online environment, including through ad hoc technological tools; information, participation and prevention to raise public awareness of the opportunities and risks associated with the use of online technologies and to create a knowledge base to foster international collaboration, exchange of good practice and information. the data speak for themselves and commissioner reding knows it well: the age of children accessing the internet has dropped significantly. already from the age of 9 or 10, children go online several times a week and by the age of 12 or 15, 75% of european children use the internet for about three hours a day: they communicate through chats, texting, and social networking sites. of course, the aim of the programme is not to criminalize the internet in a catastrophic view of new technologies, quite the opposite. the aim is to provide the right tools to learn more about and navigate the world of new technologies, to fully understand their positive potential and opportunities in terms of information, training and socialisation, and at the same time to learn how to defend themselves against abuse. we cannot ignore the fact that the latest statistics tell us that 30% of young people have had at least one bad encounter online, at least one unpleasant experience in which the child has been confronted with pornographic content, offensive or violent messages of various kinds or sexual proposals or even content that incites violence or self-harm, suicide, anorexia or bulimia. we cannot ignore the exponential growth of child pornography sites. we cannot ignore the data provided by interpol which reveals that every year at least half a million new original child pornography images are uploaded online. the commission has done well to highlight three new emergencies: grooming, i.e. the online grooming of minors through psychological manipulation techniques aimed at real-life contact. the grooming is very insidious because the approach is apparently softer. there are no explicit sexual demands at the beginning. the child is disoriented by affectionate and confidential behaviour: he doesn't understand the danger, he's happy with the exclusive relationship he's establishing, so he doesn't talk about it with anyone, especially not his parents. this is therefore a highly dangerous situation because it is not perceived as such and often ends in face-to-face encounters and actual abuse. another priority is cyberbullying, which is bullying that uses new technologies and amplifies the persecution of the bully victim who may be harassed 24 hours a day through the internet and mobile phones. and there 's another problem . the generation gap in technology. we have a generation of digital natives. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. it is therefore of fundamental importance to close this gap. the programme's objectives are ambitious, perhaps too much in relation to the available budget of 55 million but it is nevertheless a good starting point. parliament has tried as usual to play a stimulating role with cutting-edge proposals, which i do not mention because they are in the report and my time is almost up. i would like to conclude, mr president, by reiterating our commitment, that of parliament and - i am convinced - that of the commission, to never let down our guard on these issues.
the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the commissioner for her important assurances, including that the commission and commissioner barrot intend to find a legally binding definition of grooming, a common definition in all the member states. that certainly sounds like a very important goal. i believe that this programme obviously cannot solve all the problems, also because it is only a programme, it has legal limits and of course budgetary limits. but the debate also confirms that the european parliament is willing to be active in the fight against harmful content online. the future objective is also to better coordinate action at european level, by making available best practice, the most successful measures and by sharing information and methods. i believe that international cooperation in this area must be stepped up, because, as other members have already said, it is a field that knows no frontiers. the aim is to move towards real-time data and information sharing. parliament wants to maintain its leading role in this area. there are many proposals, and some of them have been mentioned by my colleagues: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. i believe that efforts should also be made to ensure that the financial transactions linked to the exchange of child pornography images can be traced. i share the commissioner's view: the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to promote the use of new technologies, such as the introduction of new technologies in the education sector, the development of information and training campaigns involving not only children but also adults, parents and educators, not with the aim of criminalising new technologies because they are so important, but they are also essential for european children.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too thank mr andersson for this initiative, with the contribution of all the groups and all the rapporteurs to the final text adopted in committee. i think that the position of the european parliament is very important, because, to be clear, it does not discuss or criticise the court's judgments as such, which are always legitimate, but it tries to react to the problems of interpretation of the 'posting directive' which are partly raised by these judgments. it is wrong to imagine that this reactionary initiative is concealing a distrust of certain fundamental freedoms, such as the freedom to conduct business across frontiers, which we intend to safeguard fully, just as we intend to safeguard the principle of fair and transparent competition. what is not acceptable is competition which may be based on the advantage of dumping. competition can be drugged by the illusion that it can violate certain fundamental principles such as that of free movement of enterprises and, among them, that of non-discrimination which, beyond any interpretative conundrum, is based on a single truth: there must be no difference in treatment between workers, whether posted or mobile, and regardless of their nationality, in relation to the country of employment, and what is lawful, including from the point of view of the right to strike, in relation to an undertaking in the country of employment must be equally lawful in relation to an undertaking operating under a system of posting. we believe that any other model of europe would be rejected and looked upon with suspicion, that free movement also concerns principles and that any derogation in this direction is first and foremost a damage to europe, even before the interpretation of a specific directive.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr vice-president, it seems to me that there is first of all a procedural problem rather than a question of substance, on which it is obviously not difficult to reach agreement. i mean, it's clear in the substance that any safety instrumentation has to go through an examination of the health of the citizens, the privacy of the citizens and the effectiveness of the measure itself, the cost-benefit ratio how much these machines cost because that's also a problem and i think that's going to become the most delicate aspect. in fact, these technologies are usually easily circumvented by well-organized terrorist groups, while they affect citizens - it is true for fingerprints, it is true for the preservation of telephone traffic and eavesdropping - well-organized groups are not afraid of these controls which instead become mass controls of tens of millions of people. i think we can agree that such a mechanism can only be given the green light by the european union after a thorough analysis of all these aspects and only after this analysis has given a positive opinion on all these aspects. as regards the procedure, we have been given a document which, in part a of the annex to document 1258, is entitled 'methods of screening allowed'. so maybe this title is what caused us to sound a little bit of an excessive alarm about the procedure, because "allowed" means "agreed to". we are asking that they be allowed only after a technical assessment and therefore a purely political decision. that is the spirit of tomorrow's resolution. it is up to you, after the political commitment you have made, to find the technical way to proceed in this direction and you will find a loyal partner in parliament.

will never be mandatory and such a tailor-made alternative will always have to be guaranteed by airports. if there is a european-style regulation, it should be like this: of course, if the laws are broken, there are obviously consequences. if there is to be legislation, if there is to be a regulation at european level, the regulation, as far as the commission is concerned, may or may not be recorded or stored. this will be in the text of the european commission's regulations. if anyone breaks the rules, the european commission will take the necessary measures. that goes for any rule, any criminal code. if a rule is broken, then the penalties are imposed by the penal code. even today, there is manual control: if a policeman gropes a citizen, he's violating privacy and violating the rules and therefore not obeying the laws. of course, he's charged and convicted after a fair trial. i am particularly committed to the health issue. i believe that all these guarantees must and can be the agenda includes the report by mrs edit bauer, on behalf of the committee on women's rights and gender equality, on recommendations to the commission on the application of the principle of equal pay for women and men (2008/2012 (ini)) (a6-0389/2008).
member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission welcomes this own-initiative report on the principle of equal pay for men and women and congratulates the rapporteur on the quality of her work. the commission, like parliament, considers the 15% gender pay gap in europe today to be unacceptable. of course, we have to be careful to take into account the fact that this indicator compares the relative differences in gross hourly earnings of women and men within the economy as a whole. it is therefore not just a measure of direct and indirect discrimination, but an indicator of all the contexts and all the disadvantages suffered by women before entering the labour market and throughout their career. the commission's communication of july 2007 states that community legislation has been effective in eliminating direct discrimination i.e. in cases where women are paid less than their male colleagues for the same work. however, they have been less effective in ensuring that the principle of equal pay for work of equal value is respected. the commission concluded that, on the basis of a detailed analysis, it would be possible to consider amendments to community legislation in order to ensure, in particular, that both direct and indirect discrimination on grounds of sex is excluded from the pay systems. the commission announced that it would assess community legislation in 2008 in terms of its relevance to the issue of pay differentials and that it would propose the necessary amendments. the detailed analysis you mentioned is underway and i cannot predict the results. to ensure its quality, the commission draws on external expert consultation and the extensive and detailed knowledge and expertise of national gender equality bodies. the preliminary results of this study will be discussed at a seminar in the first quarter of 2009 which is expected to be attended by all stakeholders, including member states, legal experts, national gender equality bodies, social partners and civil society. parliament's opinion is decisive in this process. the fact that one of the bodies involved in the drafting of the legislation expressed a clear opinion that the legislation in question needed to be changed urgently is significant. it is also important that parliament's practical recommendations for change are linked to areas identified by the main stakeholders as problematic, such as transparency of remuneration and work evaluation and sanctions. in conclusion, we share the parliament's view that such a large gender pay gap in europe is unacceptable. the commission considers that the time is right to complete the analysis and evaluation and to define the next course of action, which would lead to the most concrete results.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a regulation on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am very proud of the work that is being done in this parliament and of the ability to use the powers of legislative proposal that have already been recognised. the report we are about to vote on touches on a fundamental point, a fundamental principle of the european order: the principle of equal pay for men and women workers. it is not only a fundamental principle, it is also the first, at least in the order of time, of the principles of equality. we know that it was already contained in the treaty of rome, we know that it has been applied since the very first judgments of the european court of justice, that it is already regulated by a directive of 1975 and that it was re-regulated when it was recast in 2006, that it is the subject of recurrent analysis and research, as has now been mentioned by the commissioner, and of constant calls for its application. why, then, do we return to such a widespread and profound concern today? there are many reasons: firstly, because we refuse to accept the widespread failure to apply it, as evidenced by all the statistical data, and secondly because we believe that the excessive injustices suffered by women in all the countries of the european union and in all professions, at all levels, in all sectors must be combated, and to do this, the instruments at our disposal are clearly not enough, otherwise we would have been able to reverse this situation in all this time. and why we think that the pay gap should be taken seriously and not just as a casual event in the career of women. so, what do we ask? we are asking the commission for a specific directive on the gender pay gap, but we are not just asking for a directive, we are sending the commission specific recommendations. we have built a bridge to ferry us to real change, and we think that bridge can be very strong if it's supported by as many as eight pillars. firstly, we want to have a definition of pay discrimination, we cannot just look at gross hourly earnings, because that would be direct discrimination and this direct discrimination has actually been overcome. it is no coincidence that all the studies look beyond this, and move towards parttime work, and consider direct and indirect segregation, discrimination and horizontal and vertical segregation. we want comparable, actual, consistent and complete data. all too often we encounter manipulated or covered data, facilitated by personnel classification systems, by a work organization that is geared to the past and marked by stereotypes. we believe that equality bodies can play a twofold decisive role in combating discrimination, in raising awareness and in training for the judicial actors themselves and for the social partners. we are aiming to introduce specific sanctions, but we also know that preventive measures and actions are needed, positive actions are needed and integration is needed, and therefore mainstreaming. i hope that we in the house will accept the text in its entirety, because the more precise and detailed the work we hand over to the commission, the more we will gain in effective timeliness. and this is my wish: we don't just say equal pay, we want to make it happen.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to say to commissioner špidla that, in addition to taking into account the excellent proposals in this report by mrs bauer, if we are to have legislation at european union level against wage discrimination, i believe that discrimination in relation to pensions, even in a more subtle, indirect, but particularly odious form in a country like italy, should be included. and it concerns discrimination on grounds of retirement age, a matter which the european commission has already dealt with, and i think we must take note of it. as early as 2004, the european commission had pointed out to the italian government that a diversified retirement age was unacceptable: 60 for women, 65 for men, the most common age. well, we have as radicals with emma bonino, in every way tried to emphasize to public opinion, the government, the opposition and the parties, how this structure was to be eliminated. it wasn't done. thanks to the european commission, the court of justice finally ruled on 13 november that this discrimination was unlawful and in breach of the community rules on the treaties. the most serious thing is the kind of reasoning that italy has put forward in defence of this discrimination, saying that it was justified with the aim of eliminating the discrimination that exists against women in the socio-cultural context - that is, there is discrimination in the labour market - to remedy this discrimination another one is created, making them retire earlier than men. i think that this particular measure must also be dealt with so that it can be eliminated at european level.

year, after a performance which was still good in the second quarter of the year. all the major global automotive markets are affected, but not with the same severity. in the united states, sales fell by 32% year on year, reaching the lowest level in 25 years. the three major american automakers general motors, ford and chrysler have requested emergency assistance from the federal government. september. this is the second consecutive month of decline in china, after a 6.3% decline in august. in brazil, car sales fell by 11 percent last month for the first time since 1999. in russia, there is no fall in the automobile market yet, but there is a sharp slowdown in this market, which could experience the first declines as early as the beginning of next year. so we can see that the situation is also deteriorating in the large emerging countries. in europe, registrations fell by almost 4% between the beginning of the year and last august. the end of the year could prove difficult vice-president of the commission. − thank you for these important follow-up questions. let me say what i think is necessary. for the success of any campaign or information, we will need five elements. first, to use the internet and new technologies intensively. we can only dream of the obama campaign. i think they had usd 1.2 billion for their information campaign, but the way they used the internet proved to be decisive. therefore, we need to do that. second, we need to use audiovisual tools: 60% of citizens use mainly tv and radio for any information about what goes on at eu level. third, we need to engage with multipliers, such as civil society and local authorities’ different networks. therefore, we have other faces and other messengers about the added value of working together at european level. fourth, we need to cooperate with ‘ambassadors’, i.e. people who are willing to stand for the cause of democracy and who can reach out more than we, the politicians, can do. fifth, we need to reach young people and women, who tend to vote less and be less enthusiastic about the european union, which, not least, the referendums in ireland, and previously in france and the netherlands, showed us. these things are necessary. what about the money, then? question no 45 by avril doyle (h-0827/08) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: the european research council the european research council (erc) was officially launched on 27/28 february 2007 at an inaugural conference organised in berlin by the german eu presidency. one of its aims is to promote frontier research carried out entirely on the initiative of researchers, i.e. research carried out 'bottom-up'. can the commission clarify what is meant by frontier research on 'researcher initiative' or 'bottom-up'? what progress has been made in this area so far?
member of the commission. − here, i will be brief. the ‘investigator-driven’ approach followed by the european research council means that it supports projects at the frontiers of knowledge carried out by researchers on subjects of their choice, in any scientific field. so they have the freedom to choose. the european research council, by supporting ‘frontier research’, puts particular emphasis on interdisciplinary projects and on pioneering research. so far – and now i am talking about the progress – two calls for proposals have been implemented by the european research council, and europe’s research community has responded with huge enthusiasm. a massive 9 167 proposals were submitted by young researchers in response to the starting independent investigators grants call last year and more than 2 000 proposals were received for the advanced investigators grants call this year. this high level of participation demonstrates the appeal of the european research council and confirms that funding for frontier research on a bottom-up basis corresponds to an urgent need in europe. the commission is convinced that such investment in frontier research in the long term will substantially contribute to improving our knowledge-based society and also our innovation capacity in research.
member of the commission. − to be honest, this is quite a far-reaching question. we believe that it is important that we agree with the member states on ‘2020 vision’, because if we do then this would certainly reduce the length of further debates about what we want to do in europe. we should not repeat again and again where we are going: that is the whole idea. of course the debate is not starting now: the idea was launched with a green paper in 2000. i think it is great, especially for the new changed reality in which we live. the structure and governance of era are extremely important, and that is why we have to be patient. it is clear that we will not be successful if the member states are not in the driving seat. when we talk about the european research area and stimulating that, we do not talk predominantly about increasing funds at the european level, but rather about how we can all cooperate better – something that is inherently in the basics of the institutional framework of some of our major competitors, such as the usa, with which we want to compare ourselves. so we want to create a voluntary commitment of the member states through which we cooperate more and better than at present. concerning science policy methodologies, this is all part of the discussion which we are focusing on. i think that this question will certainly have to be addressed, but i cannot elaborate on that. i know that era’s approach is in essence one of the developments that europe most needs at this time.
question no 46 by gay mitchell (h-0833/08) subject: the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the united kingdom for the construction of a new nuclear power station. ethical review of research funding under the seventh framework programme the rules on submission, evaluation, selection and award (com (2008) 4617) of the seventh framework programme for research and technological development (fp7 - 1982/2006/ec) had explicitly provided that research activities involving the destruction of embryos would not receive any funding. does the commission consider that the ethical review of the projects submitted has made it possible to implement this policy effectively?
member of the commission. − the ethical review of research funded under the seventh framework programme is a system that safeguards the protection of fundamental rights and respect for ethical principles. in the case of research involving the use of human embryonic stem cells, the procedure consists of five steps, including the scientific evaluation, the ethical screening and review, the national/local ethics committees’ approval for the proposed research and the submission of the proposals to a regulatory committee, so this relates to which project we decide on a single project basis. in july 2007, the european group on ethics also delivered an opinion to the commission on ethics reviews of seventh framework programme research projects using human embryonic stem cells. in following the above steps the commission considers that the established ethical review mechanism has been successful in implementing the relevant ec provisions. in particular, as all research activities that involve the destruction of human embryos are excluded from the scope of the community funding, no research proposals in this area have been funded under the seventh framework programme. the ethical review is meant to verify that no eu funding is granted to research activities involving the destruction of human embryos. in this sense, it is an integral part of the whole implementation of the framework programme.

author of the book. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think i shall use less time because the subject is well known. we are talking about the pre-registration of substances, a preliminary step, the first step in implementing reach, which is very important because it gives companies the opportunity to acquire the right to interpret a transitional regime, that is to say to use the staggering of the time required for the registration of substances, a more demanding procedure, and also - and above all - even more important - to be able to give rise to the formation of those consortia of companies for the sharing of data, that is to say for a presentation made in an associated way by the producers of the same substance. so, we all know, we have been reached by information, about the fact that, compared to the initial forecasts on which the reach system was built, in fact, the pre-registrations that have been made have been much, much more numerous than expected. we were talking about a few hundred thousand - the commissioner will certainly inform us of the exact figures - but we have probably exceeded the one million pre-registered substances. and that's a problem, it's a fact that raises a lot of questions also about the causes of this explosion, say, of the phenomenon, which could also be positive. we know, above all, that this flood of data, although still preliminary and essential, has put a strain on the ability of the newly established agency for chemicals in helsinki to handle it. so the point of our question is exactly this: we want to know how these difficulties have been dealt with, how they have been organised, whether there have been any problems with the companies which were very anxious about the possibility of keeping the deadline. at 24.00 on 1 december the deadline for the submission of these pre-registrations expired.
vice-president of the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. i should like to thank mr sacconi and the other speakers for their question, which gives me the opportunity to inform the european parliament of the truly astonishing results of the pre-registration procedure under reach. pre-registration of chemicals already on the eu market is the first step under reach. it is the prerequisite for extended registration periods for the companies, which will then run until 2018. the pre-registration period laid down in the reach regulation started on 1 june 2008 and ended on 1 december 2008, i.e. six months later. when we adopted the regulation, we assumed that we would have to register some 200 000 chemical substances. in fact, exactly 2 236 625 registrations were received by the end of the pre-registration period. several thousand single applications are currently being processed and this number can be considerably increased. the final figure will be announced by the agency in mid-december. we have also asked ourselves, of course, how it is possible that the estimates which underlie our legislation have been exceeded by a factor of ten. the simple answer is: the very reason reach was made is because we just didn't know - because nobody knew exactly - how many substances we actually have. it appears that the scale of the task was underestimated by all involved. the estimates have been made using all available data from member states and industry. they have, of course, led initially to problems when it turned out that the working hypothesis was wrong. it was inevitable. under the reach regulation, the helsinki agency was responsible for defining the format for pre-registration and making it freely available on its website. in time, starting on 1 june this year, companies had access to the reach it system and the corresponding format for the pre-registration of the respective substances. during october and november, companies informed the commission that the reach it system operated by the agency was working with reduced power or at certain times not working at all. the commission has therefore followed the work of the agency very closely and has discussed software improvements and even a contingency plan with the agency. the agency worked intensively throughout the pre-registration period to improve the performance and effectiveness of the it system. in view of the rapid increase in pre-registration numbers over the last few weeks - up to a maximum of 100 000 pre-registrations in a single day - the agency has taken additional technical measures and increased capacity. these changes have improved the availability and speed of the system. however, delayed response during peak access times could not be completely avoided due to the enormous number of simultaneous calls. in fact, and this raises some questions, almost half of all pre-registration applications were submitted within the last two weeks of the pre-registration period, i.e. over one million in the last two weeks. for this reason, the agency recommended that in case of difficulties, pre-registration should be carried out outside peak times. in addition, companies were advised to use the format for group pre-registration, which is the fastest way. in the final stage of pre-registration, the agency has set up an additional quick-response telephone service to help with any problems. this action has continuously improved the response time in the reach it system despite the high number of pre-registration requests. finally, the prepared substitution procedure was used only on the very last day before registration and proved to be only limitedly necessary, since the reach it system had functioned sufficiently until then. i assume that despite the difficulties encountered, all the companies concerned were able to pre-register their substances and that the first phase of reach implementation was successfully completed.
author of the book. - mr president, i should like to begin by thanking the commissioner because i found his answers very convincing. i particularly agree with the fact that, as he said, there is also an important element to be found in this explosion of pre-recordings. we had problems because reach worked too well and it brought out, that is, a reality of unknown substances coming to the surface. i can ask a question which may be premature, since it is not yet possible to have the data and an assessment on the subject: we always thought that the system would have roughly understood something like 30,000 substances. in the light of the pre-registration, are you able today, or perhaps in the near future, to quantify how many substances will actually enter the system through the pre-registration? this is because we are also facing very significant growth here, which should obviously make us reflect on how the next steps will work.

in writing. - i vote in favour of the proposal to establish a european cormorant management plan to reduce their increasing impact on fisheries resources, fisheries and aquaculture. it is of the utmost importance to reduce the population of these birds, which take more than 300 000 tonnes of fish from european waters each year (the share of consumption of france, spain, italy, germany, hungary and the czech republic combined). the current situation is the result of directive 79/409/eec, which has led to an excessive increase in the cormorant population. the law has therefore had a direct impact on local fisheries and fishing activities, so that the presence of cormorants has become a european problem. i therefore agree with the rapporteur on the proposal for a coordinated european action and management plan, taking into account the great mobility of the cormorant as a migratory bird, provided that it is not in any way considered to be contrary to the objectives of the 1979 birds directive.

'the european parliament and the council agree, without prejudice to the powers of the budgetary authority, that the transition to the new regime for accredited parliamentary assistants will not, in itself, lead to an increase in the appropriations entered in the european parliament section of the general budget of the european union and intended to cover parliamentary assistance, compared to the appropriations entered for this purpose in the budget for the financial year 2008, subject to indexation. the european parliament draws attention to article 69 (2) of the implementing measures for the statute for members of the european parliament - adopted by the bureau of the european parliament on 17 july 2008 - which provides that the amount of reimbursed expenses for all parliamentary assistants may be indexed annually by the bureau of the parliament. the european parliament and the council agree that should the commission propose, in accordance with article 96 (11) of the cpr, an adjustment of the contribution to the unemployment insurance scheme, due to the inclusion of accredited assistants in that scheme, the necessary payments to the european parliament should be financed under a specific budget line and taken from the global appropriations allocated to the sections of the budget relating to the european parliament. the european parliament and the council recall that, in accordance with the second subparagraph of article 248 (4) tec, the court of auditors may at any time submit its observations on specific issues in the form of special reports or deliver opinions at the request of one of the other institutions of the community. the european parliament undertakes to consult the future representative body of accredited parliamentary assistants on any changes to the internal decision referred to in article 125 (1) of the cpr. the rapporteur. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, madam president-in-office of the council, 60 years ago the universal declaration of human rights ushered in a veritable global revolution, affirming the prophetic idea of the philosopher kant that the violation of a right in one country must be felt as such in every other part of the world. the human rights revolution has presented the international community with two closely related concepts. the first: there can and must be no distinction between citizen and foreigner, man and woman, white and black, christian and jew, muslim and non-muslim, believer and non-believer. in essence, it enshrines equality between all, in the claim of their rights. the second concept is that humanity itself is a guarantee of dignity and therefore no one can be treated in an unworthy manner, not even the worst of criminals. as kant himself says, we cannot deny the wicked the respect due them as men. the european union is considered the supreme homeland, the temple of human rights protection: the effective protection and promotion of fundamental rights must be the cornerstone of democracy in europe. the implementation of fundamental rights must be an objective of all european policies and to this end the institutions of the european union should actively promote, protect and take full account of fundamental rights in the development and adoption of legislation, supported by the work of the fundamental rights agency, which can give effect to the european charter of fundamental rights and at the same time ensure compliance with the system established by the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. unfortunately, the political choices of governments and the legislative activity of parliaments have not always been able to guarantee the protection and promotion of fundamental rights within the european union. the european parliament has not approved a report on the situation of fundamental rights within the european union for six years, while we have always been careful and punctual in reporting violations of fundamental rights outside our territory. we cannot just pay proper attention to guantanamo, abu ghraib, the violations in colombia and china and then turn the other way when the violations are consumed in our own home. i agree with what commissioner ferrero-waldner said today, that we must build consistency between the internal and external policies of the european union. a careful analysis of the state of fundamental rights in the european union may well endorse a bitter view that human rights in europe are often only formally protected. in support of this claim, it would be sufficient to analyse the conditions of stateless persons, national minorities, roma, the deleted, refugees, asylum seekers and economic migrants. tomorrow is the international day for the protection of migrant workers and yet the un convention has not been transposed by any of the member countries. in recent years we have analysed the deterioration of administrative detention centres for migrants, which are, both legally and in terms of the material conditions of life, real black holes, places where men and women are often treated in an inhuman and degrading way, without the necessary legal safeguards required by legislation which is often unacceptable and guarantees both oppression and impunity. the situation of human rights in the european union is not at all comforting, says amnesty international's annual report, and so we must try to promote an active policy to prevent systematic violations of the rights which formally must be guaranteed and which must be declared inviolable. for this reason we ask the council - and i take advantage of the presence of the secretary of state - to include in future annual reports on human rights in the world, in addition to the analysis of the situation in the world, also that of each member state, so that in this way - and i conclude, mr president - we can avoid the double standard. what kind of europe do we want? that is the question we wish to answer in this report, which i am honoured to be drawing up.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, there is no doubt that the catania report is an important milestone in the life of the union, since it is the examination of the situation within the union. there is no doubt that the strong migratory pressure to which the union has been subjected for several years, together with the profound internal changes under way, has created and is creating numerous problems for member states and citizens both in europe and abroad. it is also clear that the union has specific duties, such as governing the situation in the fullest possible respect for human rights, but also in respect for and protection of its citizens and of the national organised systems. however, the whole of this very long and detailed report seems to indicate a widespread appeal to the member states for violations existing in their territories and therefore under their control. the report sets out a picture of a europe which, in my view, does not correspond to the reality of things and it seems - obviously in a way which i do not think the rapporteur intended - that more is being done to those who sometimes do not respect the rules than to those who do or have to make them respected. on the whole, while i agree with some parts of the report, i believe that it should be rewritten in other areas in the general interest. finally, mr president, may i express my personal solidarity with the vatican for the attacks which have been made on it in this house during the present debate.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, our country can truly be considered a leader in the fight against discrimination and persecution, and as regards the protection of roma children, on which i think the catania report focuses a great deal, we must really thank the moroccan minister of the interior who, by carrying out a thorough investigation into the situation of roma children, has discovered a reality that perhaps could have been discovered in the past. fifty percent of roma children in these camps, left to fend for themselves, are not in school and are not vaccinated. then we should also mention in the report the responsibility of roma families who send their children away from school, who send them to do illegal things and keep them in conditions that prevent them from being integrated. so it is good that governments like the italian government, in order to integrate, for example, roma children and immigrant children, provide for pathways that allow them to start learning our language through bridge classes. we say no to repatriation when there are problems in the countries of origin. but where do immigrants come from? it is not a point in this report, since all countries have critical situations. the principles of human rights must be applied with common sense, with european nationality, not on the basis of the ideology of those who lecture us on the defence of rights when they speak in the name of parties which have the hammer and sickle of communism in their symbol. what a fountain!
president of the council. - mr president, on the 60th anniversary of the universal declaration of human rights, the catania report is timely. the wide range of subjects discussed, the strength of the proposals put forward, and your reactions to them, are all worthy of the crucial nature of the meeting we are having today. so i will try to answer the various questions that have been asked, trying to group the speeches together since many of them dealt with the same subjects. first of all, i would like to mention the question of social rights and extreme poverty which has been raised by many members, including mrs roure. of course, these economic, social and cultural rights are important. they are part of the second generation of human rights and are rights symbolised by the signing of the international covenant on economic, social and cultural rights in 1966. you are right to stress the importance of enforcing these rights, which can be discredited if they are not enforced. so the european union and france are of course mobilized in the fight against extreme poverty. i would remind you that a special rapporteur has been created within the human rights council specifically to deal with these issues, with these rights. the development of guiding principles to strengthen the fight against extreme poverty at the united nations level is currently under way. finally, the european union and france in particular have taken initiatives which i think are interesting. the european union has thus promoted and supported the optional protocol to the international covenant on economic, social and cultural rights, which has just been adopted by the united nations general assembly, and has set up an individual complaints mechanism. but of course i agree with you that this is a long-term struggle, that as long as there is so much discrimination, so many poor people, so many unemployed people, so many problems with access to health care, of course we cannot be satisfied, but there is a constant effort to ensure that economic, social and cultural rights are applied, with the european union being at the forefront of promoting them. then there is the second topic that has been raised by many, and that is the issue of homosexuality. i would like to say that the initiative taken by france is very simple, and to repeat that we started from a finding, namely that there are today 90 countries in the world which criminalize homosexuality, 6 of which apply the death penalty. this means that men and women cannot freely choose to live according to their sexual identity, and they risk going to jail or being brought to court. so this is where we are in the area of fundamental law. it is not about opening up topics, although they are very interesting, on same-sex parenting or marriage, it is not about deciding through this initiative on social debates, it is about extending this fundamental right to the universal scale and this fundamental right is the right to live freely one's sexual identity, without risking being deprived of freedom. it is as simple as that, and i believe it is to the credit of the european union, of the member states of the european union - since many of us support this project - to bring this initiative to a conclusion tomorrow at the united nations. i hope that as many states as possible will join us because, in matters of fundamental rights, i believe there is no debate possible, since it is simply a question of humanity and freedom. let us now turn to another subject, the roma issue, and more generally the issue of migration, which has been raised by several of you. as regards the roma, the commission presented a report in the context of its communication of 2 july, which lists existing policies and instruments, contributes to the inclusion of the roma population and advocates the more systematic use of these policies and instruments to promote the integration of the roma. on 16 september, the french presidency took part in the first european summit on the roma in brussels, as you know, which was organised by the european commission with the support of the soros foundation. the summit brought together representatives of the european institutions and the member states and generated a strong mobilisation of civil society. my colleague in the french government, the minister for housing and the city, and the representative of the minister for foreign affairs welcomed the exceptional mobilisation of europeans from all walks of life around this summit. this summit was important because the roma issue is of common interest to europeans and calls for a proactive policy on the part of each member state, adapted of course to national specificities. a voluntary policy of this kind at national level must in particular aim at making the roma population's access to education, employment, health and housing effective, and it is clear that coordination between the member states of the union is absolutely decisive, absolutely important. at the initiative of the french presidency, several ideas have made it possible to pursue the reflection in a concrete way. a second equality summit was held in paris on 29 and 30 september 2008. a round table on poverty and exclusion was held on 15 and 16 october 2008 in marseille with two of my colleagues from the government. in short, the situation of the roma is receiving considerable attention from the member states of the european union, and i believe that our efforts in this regard will continue even after the french presidency of the european union, i am sure, and we are fully engaged on this issue. you can count on it. so, with regard to the wider issue of migrants, i would like to mention, at the end of the french presidency of the european union, the success of the european pact on immigration and asylum. for the first time, with this pact, the european union or the member states of the european union will share objectives, will have a common position on this issue, in particular around the creation of an asylum office, around the objective of biometric visas, around the necessary action of the european union when there is too much pressure on a state, especially in the field of immigration. the pact, i remind you, adopted by the european council in october, proposes political commitments such as the organisation of legal immigration taking into account needs and capacities, the joint fight against irregular immigration, the strengthening of the effectiveness of border controls and the creation of a europe of asylum. in short, all these elements of the pact on immigration and asylum are, i think, likely to enable the european union to have a common strategy in this area, and perhaps through this common strategy to implement a genuine policy on legal immigration, together with the rights attached to it. i would now like to answer a question, a question, a remark concerning guantanamo and the consequences of the closure of guantanamo, to tell you that the european union has said many times that the fight against terrorism must be conducted in accordance with the rule of law, that is to say, in accordance with human rights, international humanitarian law and international refugee law. we also said that there can be no legal vacuum for any number of prisoners and that the existence of secret prisons is unacceptable. our position has not changed, and all this is based on our conviction that democratic societies can only confront terrorism in the long term if they remain true to their own values. and the european union believes that the united states should therefore take steps to close guantanamo as soon as possible. we are therefore in constant dialogue with the american administration on this issue. a final point, i believe, has been raised by several of you, ladies and gentlemen, i am thinking of the question of human rights here in europe, and in particular the role of the council of europe. i would like to begin by welcoming the role of the council of europe in the defence and promotion of fundamental rights. i think that the council of europe, since its inception, has done a great job in this area, particularly the european court of human rights. there are already mechanisms in place to monitor human rights in the member states, and i think that through these mechanisms we can avoid double standards and actually sweep the floor, since the council of europe and its legal instrument, the european court of human rights, are the driving force behind the reminder to the member states of the union and beyond - since the council of europe has more members than the european union - to remind the member states of their duty, to point out shortcomings and to ask them to remedy them. the council of europe is therefore an essential instrument, an essential organisation in the defence and promotion of human rights. so, at the same time, there is indeed the fundamental rights agency which also deals with human rights in the member states and which has been mentioned in various reports which have appeared in recent times. but the agency focuses on the human rights situation in the member states when they are simply implementing community law. so i think there can be a modus vivendi between these two organizations, knowing that the scope of each organization is limited to certain areas. the council of europe is not a body of the council of europe, but a body of the european union. the regulation establishing the agency expressly provides, for example, that the agency should cooperate closely with the council of europe. this cooperation should avoid any overlap, and here i continue to quote the texts, 'this cooperation should avoid any overlap between the activities of the agency and those of the council of europe'. it is therefore important that the fundamental rights agency and the institutions of the council of europe seek complementarity in their work and in the bodies involved. this is why, of course, the agency is constantly concerned with working within its own sphere of competence, while being complementary to the work of the council of europe. i think i have answered all the points you have raised, ladies and gentlemen, in a summary, leaving the european commissioner to answer the questions which concern him and on which he was asked.
the commission's vice-president - mr president, the presidency has answered questions, so i will try to be brief. i would first like to welcome what martine roure said at the beginning of our debate, namely that the charter of fundamental rights has succeeded in uniting social rights and civil rights. this is the positive contribution, it seems to me, of this charter which we will - we hope - see incorporated into european law. it's really the link between civil rights and social rights. i would like to answer a few questions about minorities. we do not have specific powers to deal with minority rights in the member states, but we can fight discrimination against persons belonging to a minority. personal discrimination is part of our anti-discrimination campaign. on the roma - i think the presidency has answered - i would like to remind you that we held the roma summit on 16 september. i myself had the opportunity to conclude this summit and i must also tell you that we, together with my colleague vladimir špidla, make discrimination against roma children a priority. this discrimination is totally unacceptable, but europe has been slow to deal with these problems. the member states have major responsibilities in this area and have been slow to address them. it is true that today we will try to use all the means at our disposal to really stimulate the integration of the roma community. that said, we are also very concerned that our strategy is not based on an exclusively ethnic approach to the roma. such an approach would be counterproductive and would negate the benefits of dealing horizontally with the roma issue in all eu policies. i also come to the question of sex differentiation. i honestly believe that the president's answer is quite correct. it is a duty of tolerance to respect and enforce this sexual differentiation. it is clear that there is a text on discrimination on this point, but we must enforce it. i would also like to say that the commission does not intend to take positions on behalf of the member states on the organization of family law. we already have difficulties in - you know - having rules about divorce. we cannot go into a field that is left to unanimity. i would add that, nevertheless, the law on the free movement of persons obliges member states to recognise certain ties which are entered into in another member state. i am merely repeating european law. i would like to say in conclusion that what i think is most important - what president deprez was saying is right - is that fears should not be our guide. it must be admitted that since the attacks of 11 september there has been a fear of terrorism which has at times led to a loss of sight of the protection of rights, individual freedoms and privacy, and i believe that this balance must be carefully safeguarded. the fight against terrorism will not be fought effectively by ignoring fundamental rights, human rights and privacy. i think we really need to get to that. and then, in conclusion, i would say that in the field of fundamental rights we do not only have to draw up texts but also to ensure that they are applied. the duty of vigilance is imperative. you can be sure that, as far as the commission and your commissioner for justice, freedom and security are concerned, i will personally ensure that the application of european law is really, at all levels, the object of our vigilance.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank commissioner barrot and mrs yade for their words of support for my report. i would also like to thank the shadow rapporteurs, mrs gál, mr roure, mr guardans and mrs ždanoka, for their active contribution to the report, to the composition of this report. i think the questions that have been raised are very interesting, and i would like to focus in particular on a point raised by commissioner barrot. at a time when the economic crisis is worsening, we must prevent a real war in the european union between the poor, between citizens discriminated against because of their social conditions and citizens discriminated against because of their living conditions, their expectations, perhaps because of the fact that they are coming to the european union and are being welcomed in the best possible way. it is true that this crisis is likely to exacerbate phenomena of racism and xenophobia, and i would like to say to mr brejc that we have analysed very carefully the report of the agency for fundamental rights and previously the report of the european observatory on racism and xenophobia, and we have found that in recent years acts of racism and xenophobia have increased exponentially in the european union. we are therefore very concerned about what is happening and we think that we must encourage processes in which the promotion and protection of fundamental rights play an active role and become the most effective link in the construction of a europe of peace, a europe committed to promoting intercultural dialogue and a europe free from barbarism. i believe that in this way, with this report, we can help to improve the role of the european union on the international scene. i will not dwell on other requests that have come up in the debate, some of which do not deserve a reaction from me, and i have greatly appreciated the interlocutory dialogue that has taken place and the proposals that have come from many colleagues who have actively participated in the debate.

the rapporteur. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank all those who have worked with me on the drafting of this report, the shadows, beyond the positions which each political group will take tomorrow in voting on this report. the fight against counterfeiting is first and foremost a tool to support the competitiveness of the european system, it is fully in line with the fundamental reasons for the lisbon strategy and i believe that it should also be considered in its legal and criminal implications in this globalised world. the oecd, in a 2005 report, tells us that about 150 billion euros of counterfeit goods are traded around the world, not counting what is totally domestic counterfeiting and not counting online piracy. some observers say that it is about 500 billion euros in real money, in counterfeiting business. a barrier, therefore, in its infringement of trademark rights, patents, intellectual property rights, of those which are the strong reasons for our industry, our capacity for innovation, our capacity for creativity. this requires more coordinated targeted action, greater attention to relations with the regions of the world and, i believe, a different approach to the relationship between the community institutions and the member states. this report has tried to focus - as an institutional duty coming from the committee on international trade - on the external aspects of counterfeiting, but the link between the external aspects and the internal aspects of counterfeiting in europe - in this europe which remains the largest market in the world, the second importer in the world - is quite clear. in conclusion, we must reaffirm some of the basic principles of the fight against counterfeiting: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. but we must also focus on the harmonization of civil and criminal rules in our internal law, and on strengthening within the world trade organization the instruments which the world trade organization has already given itself. it is clear that perhaps more frequent recourse to the world trade organisation to resolve certain problems relating to disputes that have arisen helps to strengthen the fight against counterfeiting, just as we believe that the fact that third countries outside the european union declare themselves to be in some way willing to act as a bridge for the entry of these products into europe, but also for the circulation of products in the world, should be penalized. we need stronger protection of intellectual property, a stronger capacity to defend ourselves within the world's large geopolitical areas, including the large states that face the world market, and that is why we are looking with great interest at acta, that is to say, a large international agreement within a multilateral framework, but which does not deny the usefulness of a bilateral framework between the united states, japan, europe, which also has room for brazil, india, china and the other large trading regions of the world, with a twofold focus, on the one hand, on transparency, on respect for civil and political rights, respect for privacy, while at the same time strengthening within a framework of full respect for those fundamental rights, also reasons for trade which are also reasons for us, and therefore closely linked to the development and freedom of our states within the union and also within the union itself, as a political subject in the world. i believe that we must act on consumer education, on the harmonization of criminal law, on the intensification of controls, on the use of pressure instruments too. we have the system of generalised preferences with regard to certain developing countries and we must ensure that this system is strengthened, but at the same time that it is also used to counter the bridging of these counterfeit goods by certain countries. the report therefore seeks to create a unified framework between the great reasons for freedom, the great reasons for freedom of trade, civil liberties, political freedoms and development, and to punish and tackle this phenomenon which is today creating enormous difficulties for the competitive system of the european union. we would certainly have hoped for more, in the sense that there are some issues that have been left in the background, such as the creation of an observatory and the provision of traceability rules in this report, which did not find majority support. we believe, however, that we have made a major contribution to the commission and the council, and especially to the commission, in defining in the future a comprehensive review of the rules which protect europe from this negative phenomenon.

in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall vote in favour of the report by mrs novak on lifelong learning for knowledge, creativity and innovation and, in particular, the implementation of the 'education and training 2010' work programme. i join her in stressing that action in the field of education and training deserves systematic support from the european union through targeted policies, especially in the critical areas which, according to the communication presented in 2007 by the european commission, require improvement, such as lifelong learning, including adulthood, public spending and private investment in education, school dropout, which is still too high at secondary school level, and the relevance of education to the labour market. i would also like to stress that training and education, research, innovation and knowledge transfer are fundamental to the europe of today and tomorrow and must therefore be the subject of joint efforts at national and community level.
in writing. - thank you, mr president, i am voting in favour of the report by mr deva on the development prospects for peacebuilding and nation building in post-conflict situations, which focuses on the responsibilities of the international community towards states or local groups involved in conflict. i am pleased that the amendments proposed by the pse have led to a substantial improvement in the proposal, with reference to the need for greater coordination between peacebuilding, humanitarian aid and development activities in countries emerging from conflict. i would like to emphasize the situation of children in conflict zones, particularly those who have lost one or both parents. moreover, hospitals and schools are often the targets of attacks by the forces in conflict. we must work to help children overcome post-conflict trauma, through cooperation with unicef, which is already present in many at-risk areas around the world, to ensure that children have a proper education and a better future.
in writing. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall vote in favour of the report by mrs deva on the prospects for development in the context of peace and the consolidation of the state in the aftermath of conflicts. the colleague gives a good description of what should be the ideal transition from a post-conflict situation to one of normalization of social and economic life. i think that this must be borne in mind in the resolution of the too numerous and violent conflicts within countries, especially with regard to the role of the european community and the international community. i agree with my colleague that the path to conflict resolution is easy to trace and difficult to follow. this does not, however, change the fact that action must be directed at least by the european union towards providing serious support to countries in difficulty and be totally free from hypocritical and complacent positions.
